entries.title: Treasury proposes rules defining when a payment stablecoin is issued, offered or sold in the United States under GENIUS Act section 3; comments close October 19, 2026
entries.facts: The U.S. Department of the Treasury issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking implementing section 3 of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act, announced August 17, 2026 and published in the Federal Register on August 18, 2026 at 91 FR 53368 (document 2026-16796, RIN 1505-AC95, agency docket TREAS-DO-2026-0496, 24 pages). Treasury states that it "proposes to issue regulations to implement section 3 of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act regarding the statutory prohibitions and limitations on payment stablecoin issuance, offer, and sale in the United States." The proposal would add a new Part 1523 to 12 CFR Chapter XV, which proposed section 1523.1 states "is issued by Treasury to implement section 3 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5902) regarding statutory prohibitions and limitations on issuing, offering, selling, and otherwise making available payment stablecoins in the United States." The document asks commenters whether the proposed approach is appropriate "or whether, in the alternative, these regulations should adopt an approach that is more similar to existing securities or commodities regulatory frameworks, such as Regulation S under the Securities Act," and states that "While informed by Regulation S concepts, such an approach need not import Regulation S wholesale." Numbered questions ask whether the proposed definitions of "located in the United States" and "United States" are clear and whether they are under- or over-inclusive, and whether issuance in the United States should turn on the location of the parties or on "other, broader measures of nexus to the United States during the issuance process, such as the use of U.S. financial institutions, payment rails, or other infrastructure." The Federal Register DATES section states that "Comments on the NPRM must be received on or before October 19, 2026." Treasury's accompanying press release states that beginning on January 18, 2027, the expected effective date of the GENIUS Act, a person generally may not issue a payment stablecoin in the United States without an appropriate federal or state license, and that beginning on July 18, 2028 digital asset service providers generally may not offer or sell payment stablecoins to persons in the United States unless issued by a licensed issuer. The release states the NPRM builds on an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Treasury issued in September 2025.
entries.source_label: Federal Register, 91 FR 53368 (Treasury, proposed rule, August 18, 2026)
entries.relevant_to: payment stablecoin issuers, digital asset service providers, exchanges, custodians, payment processors

entries.title: FTC announces $2.1 million stipulated final order against bill payment platform Doxo and two co-founders over search-ad biller impersonation, undisclosed fees and subscription charges
entries.facts: On August 17, 2026 the Federal Trade Commission announced that online bill payment firm Doxo will pay $2.1 million to settle allegations that the company and two of its co-founders, Steve Shivers and Roger Parks, "used misleading search ads to impersonate consumers' billers and misled consumers about millions of dollars in fees they tacked on to consumers' bills." The FTC's 2024 complaint alleged the defendants used search ads and other advertisements "to trick consumers into using Doxo's third-party bill payment platform to pay utility, car loan and other bills by disguising itself as the official payment channel for those bills," that Doxo's landing page "often featured other companies' names and sometimes even their logos," and that Doxo "did not, however, have a relationship with the overwhelming majority of the companies it claimed were part of its payment network." The FTC alleged Doxo added "delivery fees" that were not clearly disclosed and "deceptively signed consumers up for its recurring subscription program." The Commission states that "At the request of the FTC, a federal court found that Doxo violated the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act for failing to clearly disclose subscription terms and failing to obtain consumers' consent for subscription charges." Under the proposed order the $2.1 million "will be used for consumer redress," and Doxo, Shivers and Parks are prohibited from misrepresenting their affiliation with billers, from using a biller's website address in any search advertisement or using a biller's branded name or logo in a manner that misrepresents affiliation, from misrepresenting amounts consumers will pay or the nature, purpose or total of any fee, from using false representations to obtain a customer's financial information, from misrepresenting a negative option feature including the ability to cancel, and from charging consumers without obtaining their expressed informed consent. The Commission vote approving the stipulated final order was 2-0 and the proposed order was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The FTC notes that stipulated final orders have the force of law when approved and signed by the District Court judge.
entries.relevant_to: bill payment platforms, payment processors, fintech apps with subscription or add-on fees, performance marketers

entries.title: CFPB ceases discretionary publication of consumer complaint narratives and data visualizations, moving previously published narratives to its FOIA reading room
entries.facts: On August 14, 2026 the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau announced that it "is ceasing publication of unverified complaint narratives and visualizations." The Bureau states that "the publication in the Consumer Complaint Database of unverified complaint narratives and associated data visualizations is entirely discretionary" and that "Many years of experience have demonstrated that the utility of such publication is minimal, while often causing confusion and providing misleading data." The announcement states that complaint narratives "reflect negative consumer experiences and present only one side of an issue," that "these unverified allegations do not always describe violations of the law and the complaint process does not verify the allegations in each consumer's complaint narrative, nor can it, as a practical matter," and that publication "also needlessly harms companies' reputations." On the existing material the Bureau states: "The Bureau considers previously published narratives to be in the public domain for Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) purposes. Like the Federal Trade Commission, the Bureau is placing these narratives and is proactively disclosing them in the CFPB's FOIA Reading Room." The Bureau states it "remains committed to meeting its statutory obligations and will continue to collect, monitor, and respond to consumers' complaints, to systematically review and assess how well companies are providing complete, accurate, and timely responses, to share consumer complaint information securely with prudential regulators, FTC, other federal and state agencies, and to disclose certain data in response to FOIA requests."
entries.source_label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau press release (August 14, 2026)
entries.relevant_to: consumer fintech, payments and prepaid providers, money transmitters, BNPL and lending platforms
